activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: Your name written down has the same letters in the same order every time.
story:
Amelia wanted a book about trucks. Big trucks. She looked at the shelves. So many books. She could not find trucks anywhere.

She picked a book. She opened it in the middle. There were dogs, not trucks. She flipped back some pages. Still dogs. Then she turned to the front of the book. She pointed at the letters. "Dog," she said slowly. The letters were the same on the cover. So this was a dog book. No trucks here.

She put it back. She found another book. She opened the front page first this time. She pointed again. "C-A-T," she said. "Cat!" That was not trucks either. Her mother laughed. "You are a good letter spotter," she said.

Then Amelia saw a card on the wall. It said AMELIA. She touched it. Her name! The librarian had made it for her. She held up the card. The letters went A, then M, then E. She waved the card at her mother. "Look! A, M, E," she said. Her mother wrote AMELIA on a piece of paper. Amelia looked at the card. She looked at the paper. Same letters. Same order. She grinned. Then she ran to the shelves and opened the next book at the front, where the words begin.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use.
story:
Scarlett woke up tired from her long sleep. She rolled out of bed and went to find Grandma. "Let's hang the wash outside," said Grandma. Scarlett held Grandma's hand all the way to the yard.

While Grandma pinned up the towels, Scarlett looked at the grass. Something small and shiny lay by the fence. It was a little lighter. Scarlett bent down and looked at it. She did not pick it up. She ran back to Grandma. "I see something by the fence," she said. "It looks like the thing Daddy uses."

Grandma walked over with Scarlett. "That is a lighter," said Grandma. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use." Grandma picked it up and put it high in her pocket.

Scarlett helped pin one small sock. The wind made it flap and flap. "It's dancing," said Scarlett.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Holding your nose closed makes food taste less strong.
story:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She saw red strawberries in a bowl. She heard the spoon go clink, clink, clink. Mom put one strawberry on her plate.

Aubrey picked it up with her fingers. It felt bumpy with little seeds. She sniffed it with her nose. It smelled sweet like summer.

Aubrey did not want to taste it. "New food is a problem," she said. Mom said, "Just try one little bite." So Aubrey held her nose closed with her fingers. She took a bite. She chewed and chewed. The strawberry tasted plain, like nothing at all!

She let go of her nose. Poof! The sweet taste came back, strong and good. "Again!" said Aubrey. She held her nose. One bite, plain. She let go. Two bites, sweet. Three bites, sweet. "Mom, my nose helps me taste!"

"Lucky strawberry," said Mom, and passed the bowl. Aubrey took one more. "Sweet," she said, "so sweet."

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Adding white paint to a colour makes it lighter.
story:
Livia went to the art gallery with Mama. Big paintings hung on the walls. "Red," said Livia, pointing. "Yellow. Blue." Mama smiled and nodded.

In the corner there was a paint table just for kids. Livia wanted to paint a sky. She dipped her brush in blue. She made her sky. It was so dark. Too dark! Her sky looked almost black. "Yucky sky," Livia said, and she almost cried.

A boy next to her pushed a pot of white paint close. "Here," he said. Livia stirred some white into her blue. She mixed it round and round. The brush made a little noise on the pot.

The blue grew light. Her sky turned soft and pale. Livia chased her brush across the paper. Up, up, up went the light blue sky.

"That is a good sky," said Mama.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Wear a helmet when you ride a bike.
story:
Thomas stands in the bathroom. Daddy runs the water for his bath. Thomas touches the sink with one finger. The sink feels warm. Daddy says, "The hot tap is for me. Only me." Thomas keeps his hands in his lap.

Thomas washes his hands in the cool water. He dries them on the big rough towel. The towel tickles his fingers. Daddy lifts him down. "Don't forget your cookie," Daddy says. There is one cookie on the little table. Thomas takes it. He holds Daddy's hand all the way to the door.

Outside, Thomas sees his red bike. He starts to run to it. Then he stops. He turns around. "Helmet," he says. He runs back and gets his helmet from the step. He puts it on his head. Daddy claps. Thomas climbs on his bike. "Ready!" he calls.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: A coat helps keep your body warm when it is cold outside.
story:
Nora ran to the door. "Bus! Bus!" she called. Big brother Sam had his boots on. Nora wanted to go too.

She opened the door a little bit. The cold air came in. It touched her arms. "Brr!" said Nora. The wind was loud by the door. She shut it fast.

"Nora needs her coat," said Mom. "A coat helps keep your body warm when it is cold outside." Mom held the pink coat down low. Nora pushed her arm in. One arm. She pushed the other arm in. Two arms. "My turn," said Nora. She pulled the zipper. Up, up, up. It went zzzzzip all the way!

"Now I am warm," said Nora. She patted her coat like a soft sheep. At the bus stop, the wind blew again. Nora did not feel it. Her coat kept her body warm and cozy. "My coat did it," said Nora. Sam zipped his coat too. "Zzzzzip!" they said together. Then the big bus came, and it was loud. Nora held Sam's hand and smiled.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: A grown-up plugs the charger into the wall.
story:
Miles went to the library with his dad. He saw a tablet on a small table. The screen was dark. "How do I make it light up?" he asked. Dad showed him the little button. Miles pressed it. The screen lit up!

Miles tapped the drawing app. It opened. He drew a big bus. The bus was yellow. He drew a heavy elephant next to the bus. Tap, tap, tap. His finger made the picture. One little tap made a big thing happen.

Then the screen went dim. "It needs power," said Dad. "A grown-up plugs the charger into the wall." Miles found the charger. He carried it to Dad. Dad plugged it in. Soon the screen was bright again. Miles drew one more picture. Then he pressed the button, and the screen went dark. He put the tablet back on the table, just where he found it.

"Can I use it again next time?" Miles asked.

"You sure can," said Dad. "You put it away all by yourself."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Everyone helps clean up the toys they played with.
story:
Cooper was playing with his blocks. He stacked them tall, one by one. His sister Mia came in. "Can I play too?" she asked. "Yes," said Cooper. "You put one on. Then I put one on." They took turns. The tower grew and grew.

Then Cooper tipped the blocks over. Crash! They fell all over the rug. Cooper laughed. He slid one block across the floor. It went far under the chair. The blocks were everywhere. Mia said, "Look at this mess."

Cooper ran to the window. He wanted to see the wet street after the rain. A big truck went by outside. Then he looked back at the rug. The blocks were still there. Nobody had picked them up. Cooper walked back. "We played with them," he said. "So we clean them up." Mia smiled. He picked up the red blocks. She picked up the blue ones. They put every block back in the basket. "Good job," said Mama from the door. Cooper clapped his hands. "All done!"

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Saying how you feel, like "I feel sad," helps grown-ups know how to help you.
story:
Sara went to the library with Dad. She saw a big book with a wild tiger on the cover. She wanted it very much. But a boy took the tiger book first. Sara felt sad. She sat on the floor and hid her face.

Dad sat down next to her. "Can you tell me how you feel?" he asked. Sara looked up. "I feel sad," she said. "I wanted the tiger book." Dad nodded. "Let's ask the librarian for another tiger book."

They walked to the big desk together. The librarian smiled. "We have one more tiger book," she said. She put it in Sara's hands. Sara felt excited. She hugged the book. The boy brought back the first tiger book. He looked sad. Sara showed him her book. "You can have this one," she said. He smiled big. Sara sat with Dad and opened her book. "Roar!" she said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Later means some time after now, not right away.
story:
Declan ran to the block corner. Max was already there. "Can I play too?" Declan asked. "You can play later," said Miss Jo. "Max is using them now." Declan sat down. "Is it later yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Miss Jo. "Later means some time after now, not right away."

Declan watched Max stack. A tall tower grew. One block would not stick. "It keeps falling!" said Max. "Try a different block," said Declan. He handed Max a flat one. Max put it on the top. The tower stood tall. Then Max yawned. "I'm done now," said Max.

"Is it later now?" Declan asked. Miss Jo smiled. "Yes. Now it is later." Declan clapped his hands. He picked up a red block. "Yesterday I made a small tower," he said. "Today I will make a big one. And tomorrow, even bigger!" He set the red block down. The tower began.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Spread butter with the flat side of the knife, pushing it across the bread.
story:
Charlie sat at the kitchen table. Mama put warm toast on her plate. "Can I do the butter?" asked Charlie. "Yes," said Mama. She handed Charlie a dull knife. "I will watch you."

Charlie poked the toast with the point of the knife. The toast tore. Butter fell off in little bits. "Oh no," said Charlie. "What happened?"

Mama turned the knife over. "Try the flat side," she said. Charlie looked at the flat side. It was wide and smooth. She pushed it across the bread. The butter went thin. It covered the toast. One, two, three strokes, and the whole slice was shiny. "It works!" said Charlie.

"Now the milk," said Mama. Charlie held the cup with both hands. She poured slowly. One, two, three. Not one drop spilled. "Look at that," said Charlie. Mama pointed out the window. A yellow flower nodded in the sun. Charlie took a big bite of toast. "Best toast ever," she said.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: If a cake has one candle for each year, a child turning five gets five candles.
story:
Madeline sat in a big chair at Grandma's house. Today was her birthday. There was a cake on the table. It was pink with white frosting.

"Look at the candles," said Mom. Madeline counted them. "One, two, three, four." She stopped. "Four candles? I am five today!"

Mom looked at the cake. "You are right," she said. Mom took out one more candle. She put it in the frosting. Now there were five candles, one for each year.

Grandpa lit the candles. The little flames danced. Everyone sang the birthday song. Madeline blew as hard as she could. All five flames went out. The smoke curled up like a ribbon.

Then Madeline waited for her cake. The frosting was cool on her tongue. Her friend Sam sat next to her. He had crumbs on his chin. Madeline gave him her napkin. "Thank you," said Sam.

Grandma cut more cake for everyone. Madeline licked her fork. "Best cake ever," she said. Grandma smiled and gave her a hug.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Steam from a pot or kettle is hot and can burn, so stay back.
story:
Maria put on her new hat. She ran to the backyard. Grandma was at the little table. A kettle sat on the grill. "I want to see the bubbles," said Maria.

"Come and stand by me," said Grandma. Maria stood close to Grandma. The kettle went puff, puff. White steam rose up. Maria reached out one finger. "Stop," said Grandma. She held Maria's hand. "Steam is hot. It can burn. Stay back."

Maria took one step back. Then one more step. She watched the steam curl up high. The steam went up, up, up. Then it was gone. Maria clapped her hands. "I see it, Grandma! I see it from here!"

Grandma poured tea into her cup. Maria helped wipe the table with a cloth. She wiped it slow, then fast. The kettle went quiet now.

Maria sat by Grandma's feet. "More steam soon?" she asked. "Soon," said Grandma. Maria waited in her new hat. The steam would come again. And she would stay back.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The word 'five' and the numeral 5 mean the same number.
story:
Alice went to the store with her brother. Alice was hungry for a snack. Mom said, "Let's find aisle five."

Alice looked up at the big signs. She saw a sign with a 5 on it. "Is that five?" she asked. Mom smiled and nodded.

Alice held up her fingers. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." She looked at her hand. She looked at the sign. It was the same five!

She tried to walk to the sign. "This way!" she said. Her brother followed her. They turned down aisle five.

There were the crackers on the shelf. Alice reached for the box. "We found it!" she said. Mom put the crackers in the cart.

On the way home, Alice counted the crackers in her bowl. "One, two, three, four, five," she said, and ate them all up.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In games like soccer and basketball, the team with more points at the end wins.
story:
Lydia went to a big game with Mama and Papa. The stadium was huge. So many people sat in the seats. Lydia sat with her cousins too. The players ran and ran on the field.

"The blue team runs so fast!" said Lydia. She skipped in a little circle. Her tummy felt jumpy and happy. The blue team ran more than the red team. So Lydia clapped for the blue team. "The blue team wins!" she said.

Papa shook his head. "Look at the big board," he said. Lydia looked up. She counted, "Red has three. Blue has two." Her cousin pointed. "More points at the end wins," he said. Lydia watched and waited. The red team scored one more. Four! The game ended. Everyone cheered for red. Lydia clapped too. "More points win," she said. "I want to count next time!"

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Saying "sorry" is a way to show you know you hurt someone.
story:
Emilia went to the store with Dad. She wanted a big red apple. She ran down the aisle. She bumped into a boy. His block tower fell down. The blocks went deep into a big basket and all over the floor.

The boy looked sad. "My tower," he said. Emilia said, "Sorry." Then she picked up the blocks. She put them in a tall pile. The boy put one on top. Emilia put one on top too. They took turns.

Then the boy gave Emilia a block. "You can put the last one," he said. Emilia smiled. She set it on the very top.

Dad came back with two apples. He gave one to the boy too. The boy's mama said, "What a nice present." Emilia took a big bite of her apple. "We made a tower," she said.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: We feel things by touching them with our skin, like our fingertips.
story:
Chloe wanted to play the guessing game. Mom put five things on the kitchen table. "Close your eyes," said Mom. "No peeking!"

Chloe closed her eyes tight. First came a crunchy cracker. Chloe nibbled it. "My mouth tastes it!" she said. "My tongue!"

Next came a bell. Mom rang it softly. "My ears hear it!" said Chloe.

Then Mom held up a red apple. Chloe peeked one eye. "Stop peeking!" laughed Mom. Chloe closed it again.

"Now touch this," said Mom. Chloe put her hand in the box. Something was bumpy and cool. She rubbed her fingertips over it. "My skin feels it!" she said. "My skin says bumpy!" It was a pineapple, bumpy all over.

Last, Mom opened the cinnamon jar. Chloe sniffed. "My nose smells it!" she said. "Pee-yew!"

Mom laughed and gave her a hug. "Five senses, five guesses. You did it!" Chloe clapped and took a big bite of apple. "Crunchy," she said.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: Pool steps or a ladder help you get in and out of the water.
story:
Andrew went to the little pool by the lake. He wanted to learn to swim. The water looked big and shy, hiding behind the pool wall. Dad held his hand. "Let's get in," said Dad.

Andrew tried to climb out over the edge. It was too tall. His arms could not reach. He slid back down. He tried again. Still too tall. Then Dad pointed to the pool ladder. Andrew put his feet on the ladder. He climbed up one step. Then another step. He popped out of the water, easy as that. "Ladder!" said Andrew. "Yes, the ladder helps you get in and out," said Dad.

Andrew climbed down the ladder again. Then he climbed up again. He did it three more times. "Good trying," said Dad. Andrew yawned. He was ready for his nap. He held Dad's hand and waved at the pool. "Bye bye, ladder," he said.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Milk goes back in the fridge after pouring, to keep it cold.
story:
Chloe wanted to make her own breakfast. Daddy put warm toast on her plate. Chloe held the little knife with butter on it. She spread slow, slow, slow. The butter made the toast shiny. "Look, a butter lake!" she said.

Next came the milk. Chloe held the cup with both hands. She poured. A drop ran down the side. She licked it off her finger. "Mmm, one little slip," said Daddy with a smile.

Then Chloe ran to play. The milk sat on the counter. "Uh oh," said Daddy. "The milk has to go back in the fridge, to keep it cold." Chloe picked up the big jug with both hands. She set it on the fridge shelf, way down low.

Outside the window the sky looked stormy and gray. "The rain can come," said Chloe. "My milk is safe and cold." She took a big bite of buttery toast.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: Taking slow, deep breaths can help you feel calmer when you are scared.
story:
Emilia sat in the big chair at the clinic. Today she would get a shot. Her tummy felt funny and her hands felt weak.

"Will it hurt?" she asked Grandpa.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Grandpa. "Now smell the flower with me. Breathe in slow and deep."

Emilia took a big slow breath in. Then she let it out. She did it again. Her tummy felt better. Her hands felt strong.

"Look, there is a long line of kids waiting," said Grandpa. "Let's count them while we breathe."

They counted one, two, three kids. The nurse came in with a small tray.

"I can do it," said Emilia. "I will breathe like a flower."

She breathed in slow and deep. The nurse gave the shot. It was just a tiny pinch!

"Can I pick a sticker now?" asked Emilia.

"Yes, pick any one you like," said the nurse.

Emilia chose a shiny yellow star.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: It is hard to see in the dark, so we turn on a light.
story:
Henry ran to the park with his teddy. He smelled the smelly pond water. "Yuck," he said, with his nose.

Then Henry heard a sound with his ears. It was a big truck! The truck went by the gate. It made the gate swing shut.

Henry's teddy fell out of his arms. The teddy landed under the dark tunnel slide. Henry looked with his eyes. He could not see the teddy. The tunnel was dark.

"I can't see in the dark," Henry said.

His dad came over. Dad switched on his big phone light. Now Henry could see! There was teddy, down on the ground.

Henry reached in with his hands. He touched the soft teddy and hugged him tight.

"Lets talk about the ocean next," said Dad. "Can you hear waves with your ears?"

"Yes," said Henry. "And I can taste my snack now!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Morning is the part of the day when we wake up and eat breakfast.
story:
Henry wanted the dog book. The library had a big dog book. It had a fluffy puppy on the cover.

"Where is the dog book?" Henry asked. His grandma held his hand. They looked on the shelves.

Grandma found the book, but a boy was reading it. "He will bring it back later," the librarian said softly. "We can come back tomorrow." Henry frowned. "I want it now," he said.

Grandma sat with him at the little table. "Yesterday we came here and got the train book," she said. "Today we can pick another book." Henry looked around. He heard pages turning. He smelled the paper, warm and old. He found a book about cakes. It had a picture of a boy licking a spoon of cake batter.

"When do we eat cake?" Henry asked. "Tomorrow," said Grandma. "Tomorrow is your birthday. We will wake up in the morning and eat breakfast first. Then comes cake." Henry smiled. "And the puppy book?" he asked. "Tomorrow, when we come back," said Grandma.

Henry hugged the cake book. Later, the boy put the dog book on the shelf. Henry ran to it and held it tight. "Two books!" he said. Grandma laughed. "Good morning books and good night books," she said. Henry carried them both to the desk.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys.
story:
Hayden ran to the library playroom. He wanted the red ball. But the ball rolled under a shelf.

Hayden got down on his knees. He saw the ball, far away. He reached. Too far! His tooth felt loose. He wiggled it with his tongue.

A girl named Mia came over. She held a big toy box. "I can help," she said. "Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys. This box can hold them all."

Mia put in one block. Then a doll. Then a teddy bear. Then she reached far under the shelf with her long arm. Out came the red ball!

Hayden clapped. "Toys help toys!" he said.

He dropped the ball in the box. The ball bounced up. It bounced so high it hit a picture of an elephant on the wall. The elephant looked like it winked.

Hayden gasped. "The elephant wants a turn!"

So Hayden rolled the ball to the picture. The ball bounced back. Hayden caught it.

The librarian smiled. "Time to close the playroom," she said softly.

Hayden held the ball to his ear. "Shh," he whispered. "The ball is sleeping."

Mia closed the lid of the toy box, very gently.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: Zero means none, so an empty plate has zero cookies on it.
story:
Lincoln put on his blue coat. He went to the corner store with Dad. The store smelled like bread and apples. A shiny case held ten cookies.

"Can we buy five?" Lincoln asked. Dad said yes. The shop lady put them on a plate.

Lincoln counted them. "One, two, three, four, five."

Then Dad bought two more. "Now we have seven," Lincoln said. "Seven is more than five!" He saw the plate had more cookies now. Adding cookies made more.

At home, they ate the cookies. Lincoln bit one. It was sweet and a little crunchy. He counted again. "Six." He ate another. "Five." The plate got emptier and emptier.

Soon there was just one left. Lincoln ate it. He looked at the plate. He counted, but there was nothing to point to. "How many now?" he asked Dad.

Dad smiled. "Zero. Zero means none."

"Zero cookies," Lincoln said. The plate was all empty. "Zero is less than one!"

Then Lincoln turned the empty plate over like a hat. "Look, Dad! Now the plate has zero cookies on the bottom too!"

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: A blessing before a meal often says thank you for the food.
story:
Joshua went to the big hall with Mom. The sky was cloudy. Everyone brought food for the shared meal. There were breads and soups and a big bowl of grapes.

"First we say our blessing," said Grandma. "A blessing before a meal often says thank you for the food."

Joshua wanted to say it too. He stood on his tiptoes at the desk where the cups sat. He looked at the grapes. "Who grew these?" he asked.

"The grape farmer," said Mom.

Joshua smiled. He took a big breath. "Thank you for the food," he said. "And thank you, grape man!"

Everyone clapped. Then everyone ate. A dog outside went, "Bark, bark!" Joshua waved his grape at the window and said, "Hello, dog! Want a blessing too?"

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'hello' when you meet someone is a friendly way to greet them.
story:
Anna went to the playground with her lion. The lion was a soft toy with a dark mane. Anna held him tight.

A boy was at the swings. Anna wanted a turn. She hid behind her mom. The boy waved at her. Anna peeked out. Then she said, "Hello." The boy smiled big. "Hello," he said back. "Do you want a turn?" Anna nodded. "Yes, please."

Anna sat on the swing. The lion did not fit on her lap. He fell in the sand. "Sorry, lion," Anna said. The boy picked him up. "Thank you," said Anna.

Then Anna wanted to go higher. She could not reach. "Mom, can you help me push?" she asked. Mom pushed. Up went Anna, up to the sky. The swing felt like flying.

"Do lions fly?" the boy asked. Anna thought hard. "This lion can," she said. She held him up high. The wind moved his dark mane. The lion flew through the air, all the way to the top of the swing.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: Many Christian families say grace, a short prayer of thanks, before meals.
story:
William went to a big festival with his dad. There was food everywhere. There was a pretend playground made of hay bales. William ran there first. Then he fell off a low bale, right on the soft grass. He got up and tried again. This time he did not fall.

Then William's dad said, "Our friend Maria invited us to eat." At Maria's table, everyone held hands. Maria's mom said, "We say grace before we eat. It is a short prayer of thanks." Maria smiled at William. "Would you like to say it?" she asked.

William felt shy. He held his dad's hand. He said, "Thank you for the food. Thank you for friends." Everyone at the table said, "Amen." Maria gave him a big spoonful of rice. The food was warm and good. "You said it," said Maria. "Now we eat!"

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: Covering your ears with your hands makes sounds seem quieter.
story:
Blake walked on the nature trail with Dad. She wanted to learn her five senses. "You can do it," said Dad. "Let's find them one by one."

Blake found a pine cone. She touched it. "I used my hands!" she said. She smelled a flower. "That was my nose." She saw a red bird. "My eyes saw it!" Then a big truck rumbled by. It was so loud. Blake covered her ears with her hands. The sound got quiet. She lifted her hands. The truck was loud again. She put her hands back. Quiet again. "My ears hear!" she said. "And my hands make it quieter."

Then Dad poured water from his bottle into a cup. Blake took a little sip. "My mouth tastes it!" she said. "That makes five. Hands, nose, eyes, ears, mouth." A drop of rain fell on her nose. "That's neat," said Blake. "My nose felt that, too."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The counting words always go in the same order: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
story:
Axel ran into his classroom. Snow was piled thick on the window ledge. Miss Maya had a big jar of blocks. "Let's count them!" she said.

Everyone sang the counting song. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Axel sang loud. He loved that song.

Then Miss Maya said, "Axel, count the red blocks."

Axel pointed. "One, two, three, four, six."

His friend Pia stopped him. "Wait! You skipped a number. What comes after four?"

Axel scratched his head. He sang the song in his head. One, two, three, four, five. "Five!" he said. "Five comes after four, then six."

"Try again," said Pia.

"One, two, three, four, five, six." Six red blocks! Axel jumped up. "The song helped me!"

Miss Maya smiled. "Count the blue ones now."

"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten blue blocks!

"Ten!" shouted Axel. "Ten is the last one!"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Families often gather together to celebrate special holidays.
story:
Michael jumped out of the car. He ran to Grandma's door. Today was a big holiday, and the whole family would come. Michael wanted to see his cousins most of all.

He looked in the kitchen. Only Grandma was there, stirring a pot. He looked in the living room. Only Grandpa sat in his chair. "Where is everybody?" Michael asked. "They will come soon," Grandma said. "On holidays, families gather together." Michael sat by the window to watch.

One car came. Then another. Then three more! The door opened and his cousins rushed in. "Michael!" they shouted. They hugged him and spun him around. Later, everyone ate together at the long table. Michael got sleepy before the cake came. Grandma carried him to the couch, and he fell asleep still smiling.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Loud and quiet are opposites.
story:
Bennett sat in his big car seat. His baby sister sat in her small one. "Fast car!" said Daddy. The car went fast down the big road. Then the cars made a line. The car went slow.

Bennett had a little drum on his lap. He banged it. BANG, BANG, BANG! It was so loud. The baby woke up. She cried and cried.

"We call that loud," said Daddy. "Loud and quiet are opposites. Can you try quiet?"

Bennett held his sticks. He tapped the drum, tap, tap, tap. It was so quiet. The baby blinked. She yawned. She closed her eyes and went back to sleep. "She likes quiet," Bennett whispered. He tapped again, tap, tap, tap.

Soon they stopped at Grandma's house. Daddy put a cold drink in Bennett's hands. Grandma held a hot plate of yummy pancakes. "Fast car, slow car," said Bennett. "Loud drum, quiet drum. I did it!" Then he ate every yummy bite.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A grandparent is a parent of your mom or your dad.
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. Violet wanted to make her feel at home. But Grandma looked sad at breakfast. "I miss my little girl," Grandma said. Violet was puzzled. Grandma was old. How could she have a little girl?

Mom opened a big box of photos. There was a photo of a small girl. The girl had paint on her nose. She was hugging a fluffy sheep toy. "That is me," said Mom. "I was little once." Violet looked and looked. "Grandma is your mom?" she asked. Grandma laughed a funny laugh. "Yes," said Grandma. "I am your mom's mom."

Violet got her crayons. She drew Mom as a little girl, with the sheep and the paint. Grandma hung it on the fridge. "Now I am not sad," said Grandma. She gave Violet a big hug, right there in the sunny kitchen.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: If you get lost in a store, tell a store worker you can't find your grown-up.
story:
Snow was falling on the park. Andrew wore his red hat and puffy coat. "Let's slide first," said Mom. The slide was fast and snowy at the top. Andrew zoomed down, whee, whee, whee.

Then they walked to the little farm. A fat pig snuffled in the straw. His nose was warm on Andrew's hand. There was a grill near the snack hut. A man was cooking. It smelled good, but Andrew did not go near. Mom said, "Stay back. It is hot."

Andrew saw a duck and ran to the fence. When he turned around, Mom was gone. He looked left. He looked right. No red coat. His tummy felt jumpy.

Then Andrew remembered. He walked to the snack hut. The man at the counter had a uniform. "I can't find my grown-up," said Andrew. The man looked out the window. "There she is," he said.

Mom ran over fast and hugged Andrew tight. "You did just the right thing," she said. Andrew held her hand all the way back to the slide. "One more slide," said Mom. "Then hot cocoa."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn.
story:
Blake went to the library with her dad. She wanted a new book about a duck on a lake. She found one with a big green cover. It was her favorite kind of new.

Now it was time to check out the book. There was a line. Blake stood behind a boy with red boots. A girl ran up and pushed past everyone. She got to the front. The librarian shook her head. "Waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn," she said. The girl walked back to her spot at the end. She stood very still. Then it was the boy's turn. Then it was Blake's turn.

"Can I take this book home?" Blake asked. "Yes, you can," said the librarian. She stamped the green cover. Blake held the book all the way to the car.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Today is the day that is happening right now.
story:
Iris wanted her red shoe. She looked under the bed. She looked in the toy box. "Was it lost yesterday?" asked Mom. "Yesterday was the day before now," said Mom. "It is gone now." Iris did not like that word, gone.

"Is the library today?" asked Iris. Mom smiled. "Yes, today is the day that is happening right now." Iris looked out the window. The sun was up now. "So now is today?" she asked. "It is," said Mom. Iris put on her one blue shoe. She hopped on one foot to the door. Her sock got sticky from a little jam spot. Mom wiped it with a towel. "We can go now, and we can come back later," said Mom.

At the library, Iris found her red shoe. It sat on the story rug. "It was here all day!" said Iris. She hugged the shoe. "Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked. Mom said yes. "Tomorrow is the day after now." Iris wiggled her toes in the shoe. "Today, we read now," she said. Mom sat down on the soft rug. Iris climbed into her lap. "Now," said Iris, and she opened the book.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: After painting, brushes get rinsed clean so the paint does not dry on them.
story:
Oliver sat at the paint table at summer camp. He was painting a big lion. The lion had a yellow mane and a long tail.

"Can I paint the tail too?" Oliver asked his friend Mia.

"Yes," said Mia. "You can use my red brush."

Oliver painted the tail. Then the bell rang for snack time. He put his brush down in the paint cup. He shut his paint box and ran to the snacks.

The next morning, Oliver came back to paint. He picked up his brush. The bristles were hard. They did not bend at all.

"What happened to my brush?" Oliver asked.

The teacher held it up. "The paint dried on it," she said. "The brushes get rinsed clean so the paint does not dry on them."

Mia handed Oliver her brush. "I rinsed mine in the water cup," she said. "Feel it. It is soft."

It was soft like a kitten's tail. Oliver dipped it in blue. He painted a big sky above his lion.

At the end, Oliver carried his brush to the water cup. He swished it round and round. The water turned blue like the sea.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: At storytime, a librarian reads books aloud to a group of children.
story:
Brielle stood in the reading corner. She wiggled one toe inside her shoe. She was waiting for her very first library card.

The librarian smiled. "Here it is," she said. "Now you can borrow a book."

Brielle looked at the shelf. She wanted the book about the long, long train. But a boy sat near it. He hugged his knees and looked at the floor.

"Storytime is starting," the librarian said. She sat down on a small chair. She held up a funny book about a duck. She opened it wide.

The boy peeked at the duck. Then he got up. He put himself down on the carpet, right by her feet.

Brielle watched. The librarian read aloud to the children. Her voice made the duck quack. The boy laughed.

Brielle took her train book off the shelf. She put her new card in her pocket. She sat down next to the boy to listen too.

"Quack, quack," said the librarian.

Brielle laughed and clapped her hands.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When people feel sad, they sometimes cry.
story:
Aiden went to the park with his red ball. The sun did shine on the green grass. Aiden felt happy. He ran far across the field. Then he saw a girl by the swings. She sat on the ground. Tears ran down her face. She was crying.

Aiden felt sad for her. He walked over slowly. "Why are you crying?" he asked. "I am sad," she said. "My dog ran far away. I miss him." Aiden wanted to help. He had an idea. He held out his red ball. "Do you want to play?" he asked. The girl wiped her tears. She took the ball. She stood up.

Aiden felt excited. He chased the ball. The girl chased it too. She laughed out loud. Then Aiden pulled a rubber chicken from his bag. He squeezed it. It made a silly squeak. The girl laughed even more. Aiden threw the ball high. "Catch it!" he called. The girl jumped up and caught it with both hands. "Again!" she said.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: When you close your eyes, you cannot see the things around you.
story:
Matteo loved hide-and-seek at daycare. Today he found the best spot. He stood behind a short bookshelf. Then he covered his eyes with his hands. Now he could not see the toys. He could not see the table. He could not see his friends. "Nobody can see me," he thought.

But Priya walked right up to him. "I see you, Matteo!" she said. Matteo moved his hands. The room came back. He could see the blocks with his eyes. He could hear Priya giggle with his ears. How did she find him? He asked her. "I could see your shoes," she said.

Next, Matteo hid again. This time he kept his eyes open. He watched Priya look behind the big doll house. He heard her feet go tap, tap, past his shelf. She did not see him. He won!

After the game, Miss Dana called everyone for snack. Matteo smelled the apples with his nose. He touched his cup. It felt warm, not too hot, because Miss Dana poured it. "The sun can burn your skin outside," she said, "so we put on hats." Matteo tasted the sweet apple. Then he ran outside to play on the little grassy hill. "Can I roll down?" he asked. "Yes," laughed Priya, "but keep your eyes open."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A violin can be played by pulling a bow across its strings.
story:
Beatrice woke up on a sleepy morning at Grandma's house. In the corner sat a shiny violin in its black case. "What is that, Grandma?" Beatrice asked. "That is my violin," said Grandma. She opened the case. "This is the bow." Beatrice wanted to hear it play.

Grandma handed her the bow. Beatrice held it in her fist. She poked the violin with the stick. Squeak! The sound was funny. Beatrice laughed. Then she poked it again. Squeak, squeak! One, two, three squeaks. "Oh dear," said Grandma. "Watch me first." Grandma put the bow on the strings. Then she pulled it across, slow and smooth. A sweet sound flew around the room like a bird.

"Can I try?" asked Beatrice. "Yes," said Grandma. She helped Beatrice lay the bow on the strings. "Now pull it across," said Grandma softly. Beatrice pulled. Music! Real music came out. "I did it!" said Beatrice. She played one note. Then two notes. Then three. Grandma clapped her hands. "Play it again," said Grandma. So Beatrice pulled the bow across the strings one more time, and the little song went on and on.
